pos: n. (city of Castile; where the Spanish evangelical circle was destroyed by the auto-da-fe of 1559)
etymology: From Spanish Valladolid, perhaps from Arabic balad al-Walid, the town of Walid, or from a Romance name for a valley of waters.
biblical_def: Valladolid held the court of Castile and, for a few years, a congregation of evangelical believers drawn largely from its own gentry and clergy. It met in private houses, read Spanish translations smuggled in from Geneva, and numbered among its members Agustin Cazalla, a royal chaplain who had preached before Charles V, with his mother, brothers and sister. The Inquisition discovered it in 1558. On 21 May 1559 the first great auto-da-fe was held in the Plaza Mayor before the regent and the court: fourteen were burnt alive or strangled and burnt, among them Cazalla; a second followed in October attended by Philip II himself. The circle was annihilated and Spanish Protestantism never recovered. The dictionary records the city because Hebrews describes exactly this kind of ending and refuses to call it defeat: “others were tortured, not accepting deliverance; that they might obtain a better resurrection” (Heb 11:35).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an auto-da-fe as a solemn day held by the Inquisition for the punishment of heretics; to torture as to pain to extremity, to torment; and testimony as a solemn declaration made to establish a fact.
webster_full: AUTO DA FE, n. [Port. act of faith.] In Catholic countries, a solemn day held by the Inquisition for the punishment of heretics and the absolution of the innocent accused.
TORTURE, v.t. [L. tortura.] To pain to extremity; to torment; to put to the rack.
TESTIMONY, n. [L. testimonium.] A solemn declaration or affirmation made for the purpose of establishing or proving some fact.
SCOURGE, n. [L. corrigia.] A whip; a lash consisting of a strap or cord; an instrument of punishment or discipline.
scriptures: Women received their dead raised to life again: and others were tortured, not accepting deliverance; that they might obtain a better resurrection:
And others had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment:
They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented;
And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.
corruption_summary: The Castilian capital, where an evangelical congregation of gentry and clergy was destroyed by the autos-da-fe of May and October 1559.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the Inquisition and the doctrine that authorised it: that error of belief is a crime against the state punishable by fire, and that the burning is itself an act of faith, which is what the words auto-da-fe mean. Spain carried this further than any other kingdom and carried it out with the court in attendance. Rome has expressed regret for the manner of the Inquisition; it has not withdrawn the principle that the civil power may be used against heresy, and the dictionary names the principle, not merely the excess.

The principle to recover is that the martyrs are overcomers, and that Scripture assigns them the victory in the plainest terms. Hebrews lists their treatment without euphemism: they “had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment” (Heb 11:36), and were “stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword” (Heb 11:37). John gives the verdict and the means: “they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11).

pos: n. (Hieronymite monastery outside Seville whose community turned evangelical and whose monks fled in 1557)
etymology: Spanish, Saint Isidore of the field; named for Isidore of Seville and built outside the city walls.
biblical_def: San Isidoro del Campo stood at Santiponce outside Seville, a Hieronymite house of some wealth, and in the 1550s its community read itself out of the Roman church. The prior Garcia Arias, called Doctor Blanco, taught the brothers from Scripture; the mass was quietly altered, the saints' images disregarded, and evangelical books brought in by the Spanish refugee Julian Hernandez. When the Inquisition closed on Seville in 1557 about twelve of the monks escaped, among them Casiodoro de Reina and Cipriano de Valera, who went on to produce the Spanish Bible that bears both their names. Those who stayed, Arias among them, were burnt. The dictionary records the monastery because its monks obeyed a command Scripture gives twice, once to Israel and once to the church, and obeyed it at the cost of everything they had: “Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord” (2Co 6:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines separation as the act of separating, disunion; a monastery as a house of religious retirement; and unclean as foul, dirty, and in the Jewish law ceremonially impure.
webster_full: SEPARATION, n. [L. separatio.] The act of separating; disunion; disjunction; the state of being separate.
MONASTERY, n. [Gr. alone.] A house of religious retirement, or of seclusion from ordinary temporal concerns; a convent.
UNCLEAN, adj. Not clean; foul; dirty; in the Jewish law, ceremonially impure; morally impure.
VESSEL, n. [L. vas.] Any hollow utensil for holding liquors or other things; in Scripture, applied to persons as instruments.
scriptures: Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you,
Rev 18:4
And I heard another voice from heaven, saying, Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins, and that ye receive not of her plagues.
Depart ye, depart ye, go ye out from thence, touch no unclean thing; go ye out of the midst of her; be ye clean, that bear the vessels of the LORD.
Gen 12:1
Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee:
corruption_summary: The Hieronymite house outside Seville whose community turned evangelical; twelve monks escaped in 1557, including Reina and Valera.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption these men came out of was Rome's whole system as it then stood in Spain: the sacrifice of the mass, the invocation of saints, the merit of the monastic vow, and an Inquisition to defend all three. The dictionary notes that they did not leave in a rush of enthusiasm. They read, they taught one another, they changed their practice gradually inside the house, and only the arrival of the Inquisition forced the final step. That is the ordinary pattern of a reformation, and the delay should not be mistaken for cowardice.

The principle to recover is that separation from a false church is commanded, not optional, when the alternative is partaking in its sins. John hears the voice from heaven: “Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins” (Rev 18:4). Isaiah had commanded the same of those who carry holy things, “Depart ye, depart ye, go ye out from thence, touch no unclean thing” (Isa 52:11). And the call to Abram is the pattern of every such departure, out of country, kindred and father's house, “unto a land that I will shew thee” (Gen 12:1).

pos: n. (Spanish lay evangelical of Seville, c. 1500–c. 1550; rebuked the cathedral clergy from Scripture and was sentenced as a madman)
etymology: Spanish Valer, a family name from Lebrija; the given name Rodrigo, Gothic Hrodric, famous ruler.
biblical_def: Rodrigo de Valer was a gentleman of Lebrija who lived idly until, by his own account, the reading of the Scriptures changed him, and he then spent what remained of his life telling the clergy of Seville that they were preaching the schoolmen and not the word of God. He accosted them in the streets and in the cathedral, argued from the text, and could not be answered out of it. The Inquisition proceeded against him twice; unwilling to make a martyr of a man of good family, it declared him insane, confiscated his estate, and sentenced him to wear the sanbenito and attend mass at Seville, where he died. His rebuke converted Juan Gil, the cathedral's own canon-magistral, and through him the Seville evangelical circle began. The dictionary records him because the madness was the verdict of his judges and not of his hearers: “We are fools for Christ's sake” (1Co 4:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a fool as one destitute of reason, and in Scripture a wicked person; mad as disordered in intellect, and figuratively infatuated; and to rebuke as to chide, to reprehend sharply.
webster_full: FOOL, n. One who is destitute of reason, or of the common powers of understanding; in Scripture, a wicked or depraved person.
MAD, adj. Disordered in intellect; distracted; furious; also, infatuated, inordinately fond.
REBUKE, v.t. To chide; to reprehend; to reprove for faults; to check or restrain by expression of disapprobation.
SANBENITO, n. A garment worn by persons condemned by the Inquisition, painted with flames and figures.
scriptures: We are fools for Christ's sake, but ye are wise in Christ; we are weak, but ye are strong; ye are honourable, but we are despised.
Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men.
And as he thus spake for himself, Festus said with a loud voice, Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad.
For whether we be beside ourselves, it is to God: or whether we be sober, it is for your cause.
corruption_summary: The Seville layman whose rebuke from Scripture converted Juan Gil; declared insane by the Inquisition and sentenced to the sanbenito.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the declaration of a believer insane in order to dispose of him without answering him, which the Inquisition used here for reasons of social convenience and which the twentieth century revived on an industrial scale in other countries. It is a particularly dishonest instrument because it requires no refutation: the man is not wrong, he is unwell, and the question he raised need never be addressed.

The principle to recover is that the gospel will be judged foolish by the wise, that this is predicted, and that the preacher is not to be deflected by the verdict. Paul states the comparison as God's own: “Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men” (1Co 1:25). Festus brought the same charge Valer's judges brought: “Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad” (Act 26:24). And Paul accepts the imputation and redirects it, for “whether we be beside ourselves, it is to God” (2Co 5:13).

pos: n. (Italian evangelical preacher, c. 1504–1581; imprisoned at Venice, escaped, and pastored the Italian exiles at Poschiavo)
etymology: Italian della Rovere, of the oak; also called Giulio da Milano, from his city.
biblical_def: Giulio della Rovere, called Giulio da Milano, was an Augustinian who preached the evangelical doctrine openly in Venetian territory in the early 1540s and was arrested for it. He recanted under pressure, repented of the recantation, was imprisoned again, and escaped from the Venetian prison in 1543 to the Grisons, where he became pastor at Poschiavo and remained nearly forty years. From there he wrote and printed in Italian for the exiles and for readers still inside Italy; his Esortatione al martirio, an exhortation to martyrdom, was written by a man who had failed once and knew what he was asking. The dictionary records him because his history is the honest one: a preacher who broke, was restored, and spent the rest of his life doing the work. Paul and Silas in the Philippian jail set the pattern for what a prison becomes when the prisoners are of this kind: “And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God” (Act 16:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a prison as a public building for the confinement of criminals; to recant as to retract a declaration or opinion; and groaning as a deep mournful sound uttered in pain or sorrow.
webster_full: PRISON, n. [Fr. prison.] A public building or place of confinement, especially a building for the confinement of debtors and criminals.
RECANT, v.t. [L. recanto.] To retract a declaration or proposition; to recall what has been said; to contradict a former declaration.
GROANING, n. A deep mournful sound uttered in pain, sorrow or anguish; a lamentation.
EXHORTATION, n. The act or practice of exhorting; incitement to laudable deeds; also, the form of words intended to incite.
scriptures: And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them.
And suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken: and immediately all the doors were opened, and every one's bands were loosed.
To hear the groaning of the prisoner; to loose those that are appointed to death;
Act 5:19
But the angel of the Lord by night opened the prison doors, and brought them forth, and said,
corruption_summary: Augustinian preacher imprisoned at Venice, who recanted, repented, escaped in 1543 and pastored the Italian exiles at Poschiavo for forty years.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption at work on him was the Inquisition's most effective instrument, which was not the fire but the recantation: a man broken once is useless to his party afterwards and knows it, and many stayed broken. The dictionary notes that Rome understood this better than its opponents did, and built its procedure around it. The answering error on the Protestant side was the refusal to receive back those who had fallen, which Cyprian's century had already fought over and which the Reformation faced again.

The principle to recover is that God opens prisons, hears prisoners, and restores men who have failed. Luke records the sequel to the midnight singing: “And suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken” (Act 16:26). The psalmist names the hearing as one of God's offices, “To hear the groaning of the prisoner; to loose those that are appointed to death” (Psa 102:20). And in Jerusalem “the angel of the Lord by night opened the prison doors, and brought them forth” (Act 5:19), with instructions to go straight back to preaching.

pos: n. (Huguenot theologian, 1572–1651; professor at Leiden and the leading Reformed controversialist against Rome of his generation)
etymology: Latinised French Rivet, from rive, a bank or shore; the given name André, Greek andreios, manly.
biblical_def: Andre Rivet was a Poitevin Huguenot who pastored at Thouars for twenty years, was called to Leiden in 1620, and ended as tutor to the Prince of Orange and curator of the college at Breda. He was the most formidable Reformed polemicist of his day against the Roman controversialists, and his Isagoge ad Scripturam Sacram and his critical work on the fathers set out the Protestant case on Scripture and tradition with a thoroughness nobody on the other side matched; he also corresponded warmly with English divines and worked for Protestant union. The dictionary records him because the question he spent his life on is the question underneath every other dispute with Rome: whether the church interprets Scripture or Scripture judges the church. Isaiah settles the order of appeal and the consequence of refusing it: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tradition as the delivery of opinions and practices from father to son by oral communication; accursed as lying under a curse, separated to destruction; and testimony as the divine revelation.
webster_full: TRADITION, n. [L. traditio.] The delivery of opinions, doctrines, practices, rites and customs from father to son, or from ancestors to posterity; oral communication of knowledge.
ACCURSED, participle passive. Lying under a curse; doomed to destruction or misery; separated from the faithful.
TESTIMONY, n. [L. testimonium.] A solemn declaration; in Scripture, the whole divine revelation, the law and the gospel.
POLEMIC, adj. [Gr. war.] Controversial; disputative; engaged in supporting an opinion by argument.
scriptures: Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Mar 7:13
Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition, which ye have delivered: and many such like things do ye.
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
Mat 15:6
And honour not his father or his mother, he shall be free. Thus have ye made the commandment of God of none effect by your tradition.
corruption_summary: Huguenot professor at Leiden, the leading Reformed answer to the Roman controversialists on Scripture and tradition.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the Roman doctrine of two sources, by which tradition stands beside Scripture as an equal fountain of revelation and the church's teaching office decides what each contains. Trent made this explicit and Vatican II restated it in softer language without retracting it. The practical result is the one Christ named: wherever a tradition and a text conflict, the text yields. The Eastern churches hold a version of the same error, and some Protestants hold a functional version of it by treating a confession or a favoured teacher as beyond the reach of the text.

The principle to recover is the sole and final authority of Scripture. Christ charged the Pharisees with the precise mechanism: “Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition, which ye have delivered” (Mar 7:13), and said again that “ye made the commandment of God of none effect by your tradition” (Mat 15:6). Paul puts even an angel under the same judgment as a man: if any “preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8).

pos: n. (Dutch Reformed theologian, 1709–1780; author of the seven-volume commentary on Marck that closes Dutch high orthodoxy)
etymology: Dutch de Moor, the Moor; Latinised Bernardinus from Bernard, bold as a bear.
biblical_def: Bernardinus de Moor was professor at Leiden and the last of the Dutch scholastics. His life's work is the Commentarius perpetuus in Johannis Marckii Compendium, a continuous commentary on Johannes Marck's compendium of theology, published in seven large quarto volumes between 1761 and 1771: every head of doctrine stated, every historical opinion on it rehearsed with its sources, every objection answered. It is the fullest single summary of Reformed orthodoxy ever printed and it appeared just as the Dutch church was ceasing to read such books. The dictionary records him because exhaustive and unfashionable labour in doctrine is a service to generations the labourer will never meet, and Scripture never treats such work as waste. “your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines labour as exertion of muscular strength or intellectual powers; stedfast as fast fixed, firm, constant; and to search out as to examine, to explore, to seek diligently.
webster_full: LABOR, n. [L. labor.] Exertion of muscular strength, or bodily exertion which occasions weariness; also, intellectual exertion, application of the mind.
STEDFAST, adj. Fast fixed; firm; firmly fixed or established; constant; resolute.
SEARCH, v.t. [Fr. chercher.] To look over or through, for the purpose of finding something; to explore; to examine.
COMMENTARY, n. [L. commentarius.] A comment; an exposition or explanation of a book or writing.
scriptures: Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
Pro 25:2
It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter.
Ecc 9:10
Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.
Col 1:28
Whom we preach, warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom; that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus:
corruption_summary: Leiden professor and the last Dutch scholastic; his seven-volume commentary on Marck is the fullest summary of Reformed orthodoxy ever printed.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the modern contempt for scholastic theology as dry, which has cost the Reformed churches most of their own inheritance. The men who wrote these folios were pastors answering real questions, and the distinctions they drew were drawn because someone had erred for want of them. The matching error is real and the dictionary grants it: a theology that never leaves the lecture hall will not feed a congregation, and the Dutch church of de Moor's century had plenty of orthodoxy and little life.

The principle to recover is that patient searching into revealed truth is honourable and that no work done in the Lord is lost. Proverbs makes investigation royal: “It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter” (Pro 25:2). The preacher presses urgency on the labourer, “Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might” (Ecc 9:10). And Paul names the aim that keeps doctrine pastoral: “warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom; that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus” (Col 1:28).

pos: n. (Dutch Reformed theologian, 1642–1721; professor at Utrecht and opponent of Cocceianism and Cartesianism)
etymology: Dutch Leydecker, a slater or roofer; the given name Melchior, from the traditional name of one of the eastern magi.
biblical_def: Melchior Leydecker was professor at Utrecht for forty-three years and spent them defending the received Reformed theology against two movements inside his own church. The first was Cocceianism, the federal theology of Johannes Cocceius, whose scheme of successive covenant periods Leydecker judged to loosen the abiding obligation of the moral law and to invite a prophetic reading of history that Scripture did not warrant. The second was Cartesianism, the attempt to rebuild theology on the method of Descartes, beginning from doubt and from the thinking self. He wrote at length on the covenant of grace, on the truth of the Reformed faith, and on church history. The dictionary records him because the pressure he resisted is the standing pressure on every generation: the fitting of revealed doctrine to the reigning philosophy. “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit” (Col 2:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines philosophy as the knowledge of natural causes and effects, and a particular system of principles; a trust as something committed to one's care; and a fable as a feigned story, a fiction.
webster_full: PHILOSOPHY, n. [Gr. love of wisdom.] Literally, the love of wisdom; in modern acceptation, the knowledge of the principles or causes of all things, or a system of such principles.
TRUST, n. Confidence; a reliance or resting of the mind on something; also, something committed to one's care, a charge.
FABLE, n. [L. fabula.] A feigned story or tale, intended to instruct or amuse; a fiction; a falsehood.
RUDIMENT, n. [L. rudimentum.] That which is to be first learned; the original or first principle of any science or art.
scriptures: Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called:
Neither give heed to fables and endless genealogies, which minister questions, rather than godly edifying which is in faith: so do.
That good thing which was committed unto thee keep by the Holy Ghost which dwelleth in us.
corruption_summary: Utrecht professor for forty-three years, against Cocceianism and the rebuilding of theology on Cartesian method.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption is the subordination of revealed doctrine to a philosophical method, which Cartesianism attempted by beginning from universal doubt and has been attempted since by every school that has had its turn: idealism, evolutionary naturalism, existentialism, and the various forms of critical theory now in use. The method is always presented as a neutral tool and always arrives with conclusions attached. The dictionary notes the matching error, which Leydecker was sometimes accused of: a defence of orthodoxy so suspicious of all inquiry that it cannot distinguish a new error from a genuine advance in understanding, as his own hostility to Cocceius's better insights shows.

The principle to recover is that the deposit of doctrine is to be kept, not renegotiated. Paul charges Timothy twice over: “keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings” (1Ti 6:20), and again, “That good thing which was committed unto thee keep by the Holy Ghost which dwelleth in us” (2Ti 1:14). He names the alternative occupation and dismisses it: “Neither give heed to fables and endless genealogies, which minister questions” (1Ti 1:4).

“keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings” (1Ti 6:20) — forty-three years in the chair.

pos: n. (Genevan theologian, 1671–1737; son of Francis Turretin, who led the abolition of the Formula Consensus in 1725)
etymology: Italian-Genevan Turrettini, from torre, a tower; the family came to Geneva from Lucca as religious refugees.
biblical_def: Jean Alphonse Turretin was the son of Francis Turretin, whose Institutio theologiae elencticae is the standard summary of Reformed scholastic orthodoxy, and he spent his career undoing his father's settlement. Professor at Geneva from 1697, he argued for a theology reduced to the fundamentals that reasonable men could agree on, worked for a union of Protestants on that basis, and in 1725 secured the abolition of the requirement that Genevan ministers subscribe the Formula Consensus Helvetica, the confession that had bound them to particular redemption, the immediate imputation of Adam's sin and the integrity of the Hebrew text. Within two generations Geneva's pastors were largely Socinian in substance. The dictionary records him because the mechanism is instructive: nothing was denied, a subscription was merely no longer required. “they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters” (Jer 2:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a subscription as the signing of one's name, as to a creed; a cistern as an artificial reservoir for holding water; and a fundamental as a leading principle, an essential part.
webster_full: SUBSCRIPTION, n. [L. subscriptio.] The act of subscribing; the signing of one's name, as to a paper, creed or confession; attestation given by underwriting the name.
CISTERN, n. [L. cisterna.] An artificial reservoir or receptacle for holding water, beer or other liquor.
FUNDAMENTAL, n. A leading or primary principle, rule, law or article, which serves as the groundwork of a system; an essential part.
LATITUDINARIAN, adj. Not restrained; free; loose; indifferent to a particular creed or form; lax in religious principles.
scriptures: Jer 2:13
For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.
For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;
And they shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables.
Gal 3:3
Are ye so foolish? having begun in the Spirit, are ye now made perfect by the flesh?
corruption_summary: Francis Turretin's son, who in 1725 abolished the Genevan subscription to the Formula Consensus; within two generations the pastors were Socinian.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption is latitudinarianism, the reduction of Christianity to a short list of allegedly reasonable fundamentals with everything else left open, on the grounds that charity and peace require it. Geneva is the clearest case history available. No article was formally denied in 1725; a subscription was merely dropped, and the men who came after drew the natural conclusion that what need not be signed need not be believed. The dictionary notes that a confession can also be subscribed dishonestly, which was happening before 1725; the remedy for that is discipline, not abolition.

The principle to recover is that the abandonment of doctrine is an exchange of a fountain for a cistern, and that the descent is predicted. Jeremiah names both evils: forsaking the fountain and hewing out “cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water” (Jer 2:13). Paul foretells the mechanism exactly, that men “will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears” (2Ti 4:3), and the next step, that they “shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables” (2Ti 4:4). To the Galatians he puts the question that fits a second generation: “having begun in the Spirit, are ye now made perfect by the flesh?” (Gal 3:3).

pos: n. (Moravian congregation town in Denmark, founded 1773 by royal invitation)
etymology: Danish, the field of Christian, named for King Christian VII who granted the land.
biblical_def: Christiansfeld was built from nothing as a congregation. Christian VII invited the Moravian Brethren to settle in Danish Schleswig in 1773, granting land, tax relief and freedom of worship on the understanding that they would bring their industry with them, and they laid out a town on the Herrnhut plan: a square with the church on one side, identical yellow brick houses, a single graveyard where all lay in the same order with the same flat stones, and choir houses in which the unmarried brethren and sisters lived and worked in common. Soap, stoves, honey cakes and clockmaking paid for it. The town stands and is still a Moravian congregation. The dictionary records it because a whole town ordered around a congregation is an attempt, however partial, at something Luke describes: “And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers” (Act 2:42).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a congregation as an assembly of persons met for the worship of God; fellowship as companionship, communion, joint interest; and a choir as a band of singers, and a company set apart.
webster_full: CONGREGATION, n. An assembly of persons met for the worship of God, and for religious instruction.
FELLOWSHIP, n. Companionship; society; consort; mutual association of persons on equal terms; communion; joint interest.
CHOIR, n. [L. chorus.] A collection or band of singers; also, a company or society set apart.
ACCORD, n. Agreement; harmony of minds; consent or concurrence of opinions or wills.
scriptures: Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
Act 2:46
And they, continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart,
Act 4:34
Neither was there any among them that lacked: for as many as were possessors of lands or houses sold them, and brought the prices of the things that were sold,
And that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you;
corruption_summary: A Moravian town laid out in 1773 on the Herrnhut plan, with choir houses, common work and a graveyard of identical stones.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The errors to name are the Moravians' own and they are real: the choir system divided households by age and marital state in a way the New Testament does not, placing unmarried adults under a communal discipline outside their families; and the eighteenth-century Brethren at their worst cultivated a sentimental devotion to the wounds of Christ that embarrassed even their friends. Set against this is a genuine achievement, a congregation whose common life was ordered, laborious and solvent, and which sent out more missionaries per member than any church of its age.

The principle to recover is the shared life of a believing congregation, held together by doctrine and the table and expressed in ordinary work. Luke describes the daily pattern: “breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart” (Act 2:46). The relief of want was total, so that “Neither was there any among them that lacked” (Act 4:34). And Paul fixes the manner of life that makes such a community possible: “that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands” (1Th 4:11).

pos: n. (Moravian mission station in the Cape, founded 1737; the oldest mission settlement in South Africa)
etymology: Dutch Genadendal, the valley of grace; genade, grace, and dal, valley.
biblical_def: Genadendal began as one man in a valley. Georg Schmidt, a Moravian who had already served six years in an Austrian prison for his faith, arrived at the Cape in 1737 and settled among the Khoi at Baviaanskloof, learned the language, taught, farmed, and in time baptised five converts. The Dutch Reformed clergy of the Cape objected that a layman had no right to baptise, the Company withdrew its permission, and Schmidt went home in 1744; the little congregation kept his New Testament and met under a pear tree he had planted for nearly fifty years until Moravians returned in 1792 and found them still waiting. The place was renamed the Valley of Grace. The dictionary records it because the station's whole history turns on a sentence Peter had to learn at Joppa, that God made “no difference between us and them, purifying their hearts by faith” (Act 15:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines grace as the free unmerited love and favour of God; a mission as a station of missionaries, and the sending of persons to propagate religion; and nigh as near, not distant.
webster_full: GRACE, n. [L. gratia.] The free unmerited love and favor of God, the spring and source of all the benefits men receive from him.
MISSION, n. [L. missio.] A sending or being sent, usually by authority, to propagate religion, or to enlighten the heathen; also, a station of missionaries.
NIGH, adj. Near; not distant or remote in place or time.
HEATHEN, n. A pagan; a gentile; one who worships false gods, and is not acquainted with the true God.
scriptures: Act 15:9
And put no difference between us and them, purifying their hearts by faith.
Eph 2:13
But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.
Isa 56:7

Even them will I bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer: their burnt offerings and their sacrifices shall be accepted upon mine altar; for mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people.
Psa 67:2
That thy way may be known upon earth, thy saving health among all nations.
corruption_summary: Georg Schmidt's station among the Khoi from 1737; closed in 1744 over his lay baptisms, and found still gathered when Moravians returned in 1792.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the one the Cape clergy displayed: a settled church using the question of order to stop a work it had not attempted itself. Schmidt's ordination was irregular and the objection was not frivolous, but the men who raised it had been at the Cape for eighty years and had baptised almost no Khoi; the regularity they defended was a regularity of neglect. The dictionary does not therefore dismiss the order of the church, which is given in Scripture; it names the use of order as a pretext.

The principle to recover is that God puts no difference between the peoples and intends His house to be a house of prayer for all of them. Paul states what has changed for those who were outside: “ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ” (Eph 2:13). Isaiah had already promised it of the foreigners, that “mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people” (Isa 56:7). And the psalmist's prayer sets the scope of the whole missionary enterprise: “That thy way may be known upon earth, thy saving health among all nations” (Psa 67:2).
